3. Margaret Hamilton has died

Source: HackerNews | Topic: hn | Coverage: 1 source | Discussion

Summary

Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer scientist who led the team that developed the flight software for the Apollo space program, has passed away at 100. Her work in systems engineering and software reliability was foundational to modern computing. She is widely credited with coining the term 'software engineering.'

My Take

We lost a literal titan who taught us that if you're going to put humans on the moon, you’d better make sure the code doesn't crash. She built the foundation for everything we use today, back when 'debugging' meant pulling actual moths out of hardware. A true legend who proved that the most important part of any machine is the human mind behind it.

5. “Math 2.0” will need to value mathematical progress more holistically

Source: HackerNews | Topic: hn | Coverage: 1 source | Discussion

Summary

Mathematician Terence Tao has shared reflections on the future of 'Math 2.0,' emphasizing that the field must evolve beyond mere automated proof generation. He argues that mathematical progress requires a more holistic approach that values human intuition and collaborative discovery. This commentary addresses the growing tension between AI-assisted research and traditional scholarship.

My Take

Terence Tao is basically telling the AI bros that math is more than just a giant autocomplete engine for proofs. It's refreshing to hear a genius remind us that 'solving' a problem isn't the same as 'understanding' it. If we outsource all our thinking to a black box, we'll eventually forget why the answer matters in the first place.

8. The Mathocalypse

Source: HackerNews | Topic: hn | Coverage: 1 source | Discussion

Summary

Scott Aaronson has published a blog post discussing the 'Mathocalypse,' exploring the implications of AI's rapid encroachment into formal mathematics. The piece examines how the automation of proofs might fundamentally change the nature of mathematical research and education. It warns of a future where human mathematicians become obsolete in the face of superhuman AI.

My Take

The 'Mathocalypse' sounds like a low-budget sci-fi flick where the lead character is a calculator with a god complex. We’re terrified that AI will solve all the math, but we’re ignoring the fact that we can't even get our smart fridges to talk to our Wi-Fi. Don't worry about the machines taking over math; worry about them deciding that human logic is just too inefficient to keep around.
